Les Autochtones en situation d’itinéranc: Indigenous people experiencing homelessness and community workers say the SPVM regularly uses violence against them.
Frank et Sonya. Photo : Emelia Fournier: Frank and Sonya. Photo: Emelia Fournier
En septembre, j’ai assisté à une veillée: In September, I attended a vigil honouring First Nations people who died following altercations with police. At that point, six Indigenous people had lost their lives in 11 days in incidents involving the RCMP. Although none of these deaths took place in Quebec, the Indigenous people present expressed their distrust of the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM). “How are police trained? I’d like to know,” asked Ellen Gabriel, a Mohawk activist. Nakuset, executive director of the Native Women’s Shelter of Montreal, told me that relations between Montréal police and Indigenous communities “have deteriorated” since the COVID-19 pandemic. She told me that police used to consult Indigenous people regularly about how they could improve. Today, she feels that no one is listening to them. Community members and frontline workers told me that some SPVM officers were kind, helpful and eager to work with Indigenous people. However, they say that this goodwill is not enough to combat the obstacles and systemic violence they face.
Dans ce reportage, j’explore entre autre: In this report, I explore, among other things, how police officers are trained to interact with Indigenous people, how things play out on the ground, and Indigenous people’s experiences with the SPVM. I gathered testimony from frontline professionals and from Indigenous people experiencing homelessness, but apart from an interview with the École nationale de police du Québec, I didn’t get much information from the SPVM. The police service did not authorize me to interview its Indigenous liaison officer or its community development advisor, because they are not “official spokespeople.” The SPVM also refused to grant me an interview, agreeing only to answer questions sent by email.
À titre de Métis passant pour une person: As a white-passing Métis person, I have never had much trouble with racial profiling. But I knew that in Montréal, Indigenous people were more likely to have interactions with police – and based on recent events, there was fear that those interactions could turn deadly. Community members told me about the violence they have suffered at the hands of those who are supposed to serve and protect them, in the hope that police will be held accountable for their actions.
Les Autochtones en situation d’itinéranc: Indigenous people experiencing homelessness and community workers say the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) regularly uses violence and commits abuses against Indigenous people. Although the SPVM has added new training to its program, frontline workers say it isn’t working.
La Converseest allée à la rencontre de S: La Converse met with Steven Martin and Diane, two First Nations people without a fixed address. Both have had interactions with the SPVM in which they felt “degraded” and “racially profiled.” They are housed in an Indigenous shelter in the Plateau-Mont-Royal, where, they say, police violence is commonplace.
<strong>« Je n’avais jamais fait l’objet: “I had never been racially profiled before”
Diane est une femme crie-métisse d’une c: Diane is a Cree-Métis woman in her fifties from Buffalo Lake, a Métis settlement in Alberta. Wanting to be closer to her daughter, who lives with her father, Diane’s ex-husband, she left Edmonton to settle in Montréal two years ago. Unable to keep living with her ex, Diane ended up on the street and was referred to a shelter. She has light eyes, olive skin and a soft voice. Diane puts her education to use to help the community at the shelter where she is staying, doing their taxes and helping them fill out compensation claims for the Sixties Scoop. Although she says she doesn’t resist police, Diane says she knows her rights and will question police if she feels they are being unreasonable.
En mai 2024, Diane est assise sur un ban: In May 2024, Diane was sitting on a bench in the Plateau-Mont-Royal with a friend when two SPVM officers approached them. Diane’s friend was intoxicated, but neither of them was drinking alcohol in public. Speaking in English, Diane says the officers began belittling her friend and told them they had to leave because it was private property.
« Je n’étais pas ivre et je n’étais pas: “I wasn’t drunk and I wasn’t being aggressive or anything. I just said, ‘This is a public thoroughfare. Show me the signs that say we’re not allowed to sit here,’” says Diane, speaking quickly as the memories come back to her.
Les agents lui parlent en français – l’a: The officers spoke to her in French – Diane’s friend translated what they were saying so she could understand what was going on. “I told them, ‘Hey, you haven’t had cultural sensitivity training. You obviously need it.’ And they said, ‘One more word and we’ll handcuff you and put you in a car,’” she recalls.
Diane raconte que les agents l’ont menot: Diane says the officers handcuffed her and put her in the back of their patrol car, but did not take her to the police station.
« Je me suis dit : \"C’est sûr, je vais: “I thought, ‘For sure, I’m going to jail.’ But they drove me to a block and let me out near the Saint-Laurent metro station. I was pleasantly surprised, but I was bewildered,” says Diane.
Selon les résidents et les travailleurs: According to residents and workers at the shelter, it’s a spot where drug dealers known to police hang out. Steven Martin suspects that this is why the officers let Diane out there, and that they tried to embarrass her by making sure people saw her getting out of a police car in handcuffs.
« Si un trafiquant de drogue passe par l: “If a drug dealer walks by and sees her getting out of the police car, it’s even more shameful, he wonders whether he can still trust her. The first thing they think is, ‘Maybe she’s ratting us out,’” explains Mr. Martin.
Diane raconte qu’après lui avoir passé l: Diane says that after handcuffing her, the officers handed her a notice written entirely in French. When she asked them what it was, they told her, “Figure it out,” this time speaking in English. Four months later, she received a second notice, this time in French and English, stating that she was fined $757 – $500 for the original offence, plus $257 in late fees – for “taking part in a fight or other act of physical violence in the public domain or in an area adjacent to the public domain.”
Lorsqu’elle a demandé à quelqu’un du ref: When she asked someone at the shelter to translate the charges – the only part of the notice that wasn’t translated into English – she was even more shocked. “I wasn’t violent, but it made it sound like I was assaulting people or something,” says Diane, upset.
Diane a déjà eu des démêlés avec des pol: Diane has had run-ins with police before, when she lived in Edmonton. She says that in all her dealings with police, including when she was arrested, she had never felt disrespected until she dealt with SPVM officers. “I had never been racially profiled until that moment, and it was very humiliating,” says Diane.
M. Martin lui suggère de porter son hist: Mr. Martin suggests she take her story to court. “The judge will rule in your favour anyway. I mean, you didn’t do anything wrong,” he advises, before telling me about his own recent experience with the SPVM.
<strong>« Laissez-moi partir. Lâchez-moi: “Let me go. Get off me. I can’t breathe.”
Steven Martin, un Mi’kmaq originaire de: Steven Martin, a Mi’kmaq from Burnt Church, New Brunswick, has lived in Montréal on and off for about ten years. He has travelled a lot, doesn’t hide his drug use, is adventurous and doesn’t mince words.
« Le profilage racial existe. Les agents: “Racial profiling exists. SPVM officers refuse to speak to me in English. Me, I get worked up. I’m not like Diane. I tell them to go fuck themselves, to talk to me in English; if you don’t talk to me in English, I don’t understand anything,” he says in English.
M. Martin a également eu une altercation: Mr. Martin also had a confrontation with police when he was sitting in a public place and officers ordered him to move. In early 2024, he was sitting at Place de la Paix, on Saint-Laurent Boulevard, with a group of Indigenous people. SPVM officers approached his group and told them they weren’t allowed to sit there, even though another group of non-Indigenous people was sitting in the same park.
Il rapporte avoir dit aux agents : « Je: He says he told the officers: “I don’t see a goddamn sign here [saying we can’t sit here]. I only speak English. I don’t speak French, and you’re talking among yourselves. So how am I supposed to know what you’re going to do to me?”
Un agent demande alors à M. Martin une p: One officer then asks Mr. Martin for ID. He explains that he left it at the shelter. The officer replies that he will arrest him if he doesn’t have ID on him. Mr. Martin then blurts out: “Arrest me. I don’t care. I’m not doing anything wrong. I’m just sitting here. Why do you want to arrest me?” “Because you don’t have ID.” “So I said, ‘Arrest me, because I don’t have ID.’”
Les agents lui passent les menottes et l: The officers handcuff him and put him in the back of their vehicle, then do the same thing they did with Diane: they drop him off a block away, near where the drug dealers hang out and where passersby can see him getting out of the patrol car in handcuffs.
« Je criais à l’arrière de la voiture ;: “I was yelling in the back of the car; everyone was looking at me. I called them all a bunch of fucking assholes who were racially profiling me. And they were laughing at me!” says Mr. Martin, growing agitated as he recalls the memory. “They told me I needed ID or I’d get arrested. That’s why I lost it, because I know I’m not breaking any law,” he says.
En août 2024, il s’est battu avec un ind: In August 2024, he got into a fight with someone in the Plateau-Mont-Royal. Injured and limping, he made his way to the corner of Sherbrooke and Saint-Urbain streets. He says he had a concussion and broken ribs. When they saw him, someone called the police.
Il déclare que les policiers l’ont jeté: He says the officers threw him to the ground and handcuffed him behind his back. Mr. Martin says he was lying on his back with an officer sitting on his legs, and the officers began putting pressure on his injuries.
« L’un d’eux a mis son genou sur ma poit: “One of them put his knee on my chest, right where my ribs were broken,” he says, pointing to the left side of his rib cage. “The other put his knee on my head, where I had the concussion.” He presses his other hand against the side of his head, stretching and twisting. “I was screaming, I was howling, and all of a sudden, I passed out,” says Mr. Martin, who reenacts the scene, slumping in his chair and closing his eyes.
Il raconte qu’il a été réveillé par quel: He says he was woken up by someone pressing on a spot in his upper back. “I started panicking again. I said, ‘What the hell are you doing! I have broken ribs, I have a concussion, what are you doing?’ All of a sudden, a cop put his knee on my chest again, and the other one put his knee on my fucking head. I collapsed again. I passed out from the pain,” he says.
Ce cycle s’est répété et M. Martin a dit: This cycle repeated, and Mr. Martin told the officers: “Let me go. Let me get up. I can’t breathe.”
« Je délirais à cause de la douleur et p: “I was delirious from the pain and because I didn’t know what was going on. Then I looked up, and the cop said to me, ‘Do you want me to do it again?’ I answered, ‘You’re putting me through so much suffering right now. I don’t give a fuck anymore. Do it again. I don’t care.’ Suddenly, the ambulance arrived. Everyone moved away from me so it would look good. I told the paramedic, ‘They messed me up.’”
There was no follow-up to this incident.
En l’absence de numéro d’événement, de d: Without an event number, a specific date or a direct witness, the relevant neighbourhood police station said it could not confirm that there had been a police intervention involving Steven Martin at that location in August 2024. La Converse is investigating the incident.
Environ un mois plus tard, M. Martin a e: About a month later, Mr. Martin had another interaction with SPVM officers in an alley in the Plateau, where they accused him of urinating in public, which he denies. They told him they would fine him for public urination and ordered him to “sit down” where they thought he had urinated.
« Vous voulez me rabaisser et m’obliger: “You want to degrade me and force me to sit in a spot where you think I pissed? I said, ‘You can all go fuck yourselves!’” says Mr. Martin. A worker at the shelter confirmed the incident. The police did not give him a fine.
<strong>« Je préfère être frappée au vis: “I’d rather be hit in the face than have to call the police”
Marie*, une intervenante qui travaille d: Marie*, a frontline worker at a reception centre for Indigenous people in Montréal, says she has heard and witnessed many stories like Steven’s and Diane’s: officers who refuse to speak English, who use excessive force, who handcuff Indigenous people and then drop them off nearby, who hand out fines that seem unjustified, and so on.
À l’endroit où elle travaille, appeler l: Where she works, calling the police is a last resort when the safety of workers and other residents is seriously threatened. Marie prefers to call Urgence psychosociale, but if the person in crisis is deemed “aggressive,” she is told to call the police.
« Je préfère être frappée au visage plut: “I’d rather be hit in the face than have to call the police,” she says.
« Chaque fois qu’il faut appeler les age: “Every time we have to call the officers, we see people being dragged across the ground, which is never a good procedure. If two big men are able to carry someone, they can put them in the car properly. I’ve seen people get kicked, get hit with Tasers... Why do police resort so quickly to violence and lethal methods when it comes to members of the community?” says Marie indignantly.
Selon elle, la violence de nombreux rési: In her view, the violence of many shelter residents stems from trauma and addiction. They need a mental health intervention, not police violence. While Marie says she has met “good cops,” she points out that there is no way of knowing what kind of behaviour they will adopt, which leads Indigenous residents to be wary when they see police in uniform.
« Ici, ils sont sur la défensive, ils vo: “Here, they’re on the defensive, they’re going to try to protect their own. They’re going to try to make sure that what happened to those who were killed or assaulted doesn’t happen to them,” she says.
Dans un courriel adressé à La Converse,: In an email to La Converse, the SPVM said that it generally does not comment on its interventions “in order to prevent any influence on a possible judicial, ethics or disciplinary process.” It did specify, however, that officers are expected to “reach a functional level of spoken English.” When we responded that there were numerous accounts from Indigenous people who were spoken to exclusively in French and who were handcuffed and released a few blocks away in front of drug dealers, the SPVM said: “After verification, no incident of this nature has been reported to us.”
<strong>Pourquoi utiliser des Tasers ? P: Why use Tasers? Why use firearms? Why not try dialogue?
Les violences policières contre les Auto: Police violence against Indigenous people is <l1>a recurring phenomenon in Canada</l1>.
Du 29 août au 25 septembre 2024, <l1>neu: Between August 29 and September 25, 2024, <l1>nine First Nations people</l1> died after altercations with police services in Canada: <l2>Jack Charles Piche</l2>, 31; <l3>Hoss Lightning Saddleback</l3>, 15, of Samson Cree First Nation; <l4>Tammy Bateman</l4>, 39, of Roseau River Anishinaabe First Nation; <l5>Jason West</l5>, 57; <l6>Danny Knife</l6>, 31, of Atahkakoop Cree Nation; <l7>Steven “Iggy” Dedam</l7>, 34, of Elsipogtog First Nation; <l8>Jon Wells</l8>, 42, of Blood Tribe; <l9>Ronald Skunk</l9>, 59, a member of Mishkeegogamang; and <l10>Joseph Desjarlais</l10>, 34, of Fishing Lake Cree Nation.
En novembre dernier, <l1>la police du Nu: Last November, <l1>Nunavik police</l1> shot and killed Joshua Papigatuk, a 27-year-old Inuk man, and seriously injured his twin brother, Garnet, in Salluit, in northern Quebec.
En janvier, le procès de <l1>l’agent du: In January, the trial of <l1>SPVM officer Williams Bélanger</l1> opened at the Superior Court in Montréal. He is charged with assaulting Johnny Inukpak Tukaluk, an Inuk man experiencing homelessness, in the Plateau in May 2022. Mr. Bélanger was charged with assault following an investigation by the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes (BEI), Quebec’s police oversight body. Since 2018, <l2>the BEI automatically investigates</l2> whenever the victim or complainant is Indigenous.
M. Tukalak est mort d’une overdose l’aut: Mr. Tukaluk died of an overdose last fall before the trial began, but friends and frontline workers said he suffered brain damage after Officer Bélanger allegedly pushed him and struck his head on the concrete.
La Converse s’est entretenue avec Sonya: La Converse spoke with Sonya Gagnier of the <l1>Native Para-Judicial Services of Quebec</l1> (SPAQ) during the first part of Williams Bélanger’s trial, which will resume in March. Ms.<sup> </sup>Gagnier, a Mohawk from Kahnesatake, and her Algonquin colleague Frank Wabbie attended the trial as part of the SPAQ’s mandate. Their work involves helping Indigenous people navigate the justice system and ensuring their rights are protected.
Aux dires de M<sup>me </sup>Gagnier, des: According to Ms.<sup> </sup>Gagnier, cases like Mr. Tukaluk’s are an enormous setback for relations between Indigenous people and police. “When something happens to one [Indigenous person], it affects everyone. People think the police are bad, they killed my friend, they hurt my friend,” she says.
M<sup>me </sup>Gagnier et M. Wabbie sont: Ms.<sup> </sup>Gagnier and Mr. Wabbie are responsible for all SPAQ clients in Montréal and Saint-Jérôme. Ms.<sup> </sup>Gagnier estimates that between the two of them, they handle about 800 Indigenous clients facing legal problems. Many are experiencing homelessness. During the interview Ms.<sup> </sup>Gagnier gave La Converse at the SPAQ’s head office in Montréal, her phone rang often, and she had to stop several times to answer clients she had been trying to reach for some time.
Selon elle, le nombre disproportionné de: In her view, the disproportionate number of Indigenous people experiencing homelessness is attributable to factors whose effects are cumulative. The lack of jobs and housing in communities pushes people toward regions farther south; and a history tied to colonialism, trauma and addiction, combined with culture shock and a housing crisis, can lead them to the street. Ms.<sup> </sup>Gagnier explains that many of her clients are stuck in a “revolving door” between court, prison and the street. Often, release conditions prohibit alcohol consumption and require people to complete a treatment program and stay out of trouble – which is hard to do when resources are limited.
« Le tribunal demande qu’ils suivent une: “The court asks that they go into a closed-setting therapy program, and if they can’t, and if they don’t have certain guarantees like a stable place to live, they end up in jail because they can’t meet the court’s demand. So you’re back to square one: the client goes back to jail and waits for their trial,” explains M<sup>s</sup>. Gagnier.
Selon elle, rares sont les services de t: According to her, few addiction and rehabilitation services in Montréal offer treatment that is culturally adapted to First Nations and Inuit people. And those that have space aren’t comprehensive enough. “If they’ve been drinking since they were 16 and they’re now 45, six weeks isn’t enough. We all know it only serves to appease the court to a certain extent, but does it really help the person in the end?” she asks.
Cette année, les organisations locales o: This year, local organizations have reported an increase in the number of Indigenous people without safe housing, says M<sup>s</sup>. Gagnier. According to SPAQ data, Montréal’s homeless population rose from 3,000 to 5,000 people between 2016 and 2025. In 2022, Indigenous people made up 13% of Montréal’s homeless population, even though they account for only about 2.5% of Quebec’s population. The growing number of Indigenous people experiencing homelessness is putting added pressure on services like SPAQ and the <l1>Centre de justice des premiers peuples de Montréal</l1>, as well as on frontline workers.
Nakuset s'adressant à la foule présente: Nakuset addresses the crowd at a vigil for Indigenous people who died following incidents with police. Photo: Emelia Fournier
« Tout le monde s’épuise parce que nous: “Everyone is burning out because we’re stretched to the limit... We hear people’s stories and their trauma, we absorb it, and we don’t get the chance to take stock,” she says.
M<sup>me </sup>Gagnier a tenté de trouve: M<sup>s</sup>. Gagnier has tried to find a compromise with the courts so that clients are held until a spot opens up at a treatment centre. She has also asked lawyers to make sure their clients fully understand the conditions of their release, which are explained to them in French, often to no avail.
« J’ai fondu en larmes devant le juge à: “I’ve broken down in tears in front of the judge several times while trying to express how frustrating this situation is to deal with,” she laments.
M<sup>me </sup>Gagnier explique que les: M<sup>s</sup>. Gagnier explains that Indigenous people experiencing homelessness are more likely to have interactions with police and the justice system – and that these interactions often become explosive, and quickly.
« Oui, il arrive que nos clients perdent: “Yes, sometimes our clients lose their cool. But there are ways to deal with that without resorting to force. Police officers are well enough trained – you hear them bragging about knowing how to use pressure points [to subdue someone]; so why not use them? Why use Tasers, why use firearms, why not try talking, why not say, ‘Calm down, this is why I’m arresting you’?” says M<sup>s</sup>. Gagnier.
Si le SPVM a décliné toute demande d’ent: While the SPVM declined all interview requests, it pointed out by email that it offers evolving training programs to its officers. “From the moment he took the helm of the SPVM [in December 2022], Director Dagher committed to fighting discrimination in all its forms... Is everything the SPVM does perfect? No. There will always be room for improvement,” SPVM communications manager Caroline Labelle said by email.
Le SPVM dispose d’un conseiller en dével: The SPVM has a community development advisor and an Indigenous liaison officer, who act as a link between community organizations and the SPVM and who train police officers.
Les nouvelles recrues sont davantage <l1: New recruits are getting more <l1>training in the field</l1> through the <l2>SPVM’s Immersion MTL program</l2>, an initiative of police chief Fady Dagher launched in August 2022. For five weeks, officers in the program accompany frontline workers to learn how to handle situations involving people experiencing homelessness and mental health issues.
À l’<l1>École nationale de la police du: At the <l1>École nationale de la police du Québec (ENPQ)</l1>, where Quebec police officers receive their initial training, the number of training hours on racial profiling and Indigenous realities has been increased. Indigenous organizations such as Femmes autochtones du Québec and SPAQ step in to train officers at every stage of their careers.
« Au cours de la carrière des agents, il: “Throughout officers’ careers, it’s important to have ongoing training and refreshers, particularly on social issues,” said Véronique Brunet, head of communications at the ENPQ, in a phone interview with La Converse.
En 2023, l’ENPQ a lancé de <l1>nouveaux: In 2023, the ENPQ launched <l1>new training programs</l1> for serving officers, including on racial profiling and unconscious bias.
<strong>La Converse a déposé une demande: La Converse filed an access to information request to learn more about this new training. The content of the program is protected by intellectual property rights. However, we obtained the names of the organizations and individuals who took part in developing the program or who were consulted during the process. No Indigenous organizations appear among those names.
Interrogés sur la raison de l’absence d’: Asked why Indigenous organizations were absent from the list, the ENPQ said:
« Le contenu du programme d’activités de: “The content of the training program on racism and racial and social profiling must meet general objectives that were previously established with partners (ENPQ, MSP, CDPDJ, Police Ethics Commissioner). That is why there are no members of Indigenous communities on the list of contributors who took part in developing the modules.”
Il n’a pas indiqué si l’une ou l’autre d: It did not say whether any of the people named were Indigenous.
Le programme de formation initiale de l’: The ENPQ’s initial training program includes 11 hours of instruction on “diversity, profiling and Indigenous realities,” which includes “various training activities, simulated scenarios, police ride-alongs and classroom discussions.” According to M<sup>s</sup>. Brunet, students practise intervening in simulated conflicts to sharpen their skills as part of what she calls “training in action.”
« Le point le plus enrichissant de ces s: “The most valuable part of these scenarios, these simulations, is obviously seeing the candidate in action, but it’s also, of course, the feedback that follows,” said M<sup>s</sup>. Brunet.
Mais ce n’est pas la même chose que l’ac: But it’s not the same as acting in the field. In an article by Jesse Feith in <l1>The Gazette</l1>, a 23-year-old recruit said after going through the Immersion MTL experience: “I think we were a bit coddled in CEGEP and at police school. We weren’t confronted with the reality we’re going to be working with.”
L’ENPQ et le SPVM ont tous deux déclaré: Both the ENPQ and the SPVM said they were open to dialogue with Indigenous communities and frontline workers. However, according to community members, dialogue has been at a standstill for some time.
Depuis des années, ces derniers demanden: For years, they have been calling for an end to the practice of police stops, in which an officer stops a citizen to ask for information without valid reason. Although SPVM chief Fady Dagher has acknowledged the existence of systemic racism, he <l1>still refuses to ban police stops</l1>. He has, however, put in place a policy stating that <l2>these stops are to be carried out in a non-discriminatory manner</l2> – but that isn’t possible given their very nature, according to <l3>multiple studies</l3>.
En 2021, les Autochtones étaient <l1>six: In 2021, Indigenous people were <l1>six times more likely to be stopped</l1> than white people, which increased how often they interacted with police.
En décembre, <l1>la Ville de Montréal a: In December, <l1>the City of Montréal held a public meeting</l1> on the practice of police stops. Two groups of researchers found the practice to be racist, and the citizens who showed up to the meeting denounced it. The SPVM had no representative at the meeting, although it had officers posted outside the venue.
Même si elle entrevoit un avenir de coll: Although she envisions a future of collaboration with police, M<sup>s</sup>. Gagnier believes the current training model isn’t working. “The SPVM currently has an excellent team that is making a lot of effort,” she says. While Immersion MTL seems to be a step in the right direction, only new recruits get this five-week training. “The training models are pretty boring and they always come back with the same thing,” says M<sup>s</sup>. Gagnier, who has led Indigenous sensitivity training sessions. “Some officers have taken this training over and over, and you can read on their faces that they’re thinking, ‘Here we go, they’re going to talk about purification…’”
« La police doit faire le travail d’inte: “Police need to do outreach work in shelters alongside social workers, they need hands-on training, training in the field. Officers need to spend time with these people. I would even go as far as sending them up North for a month to spend time with the Inuit and learn about their way of life, so that they really understand how to help them here,” she adds.
Selon M<sup>me </sup>Gagnier, les polici: According to M<sup>s</sup>. Gagnier, police officers need mental health support and rest, just like outreach workers and frontline workers. “They shouldn’t stay out in the field too long; they should have a less harsh, less intense assignment to do. They’re human, like everyone else. That doesn’t excuse the deplorable behaviour they choose to adopt, but they need to be able to say they’ve reached their breaking point,” she explains.
Marie affirme que la culture policière d: Marie says police culture must change and that the consequences for excessive use of force must go beyond a paid suspension and apologies. “Some officers have come to see me and told me they didn’t agree with the way things went down, or that they had heard about what happened and were sorry. The problem is, they’ll never go to the officer who did it and say, ‘That was too much, you were too violent, you shouldn’t have grabbed her like that, she needed mental health support and you were violent.’”
Marie affirme également que le refuge a: Marie also says the shelter needs more mental health and addiction workers. If officers could come in plain clothes, accompanied by a mental health support team, the reaction might be more positive.
« Souvent, les gens agissent de manière: “Often, people act in a disorderly way because they’re going through something so emotionally overwhelming that they don’t know how to express it,” she explains. “Ideally, we would never have to deal with police at all.”
